name: The Shirky Principle
statement: Institutions will try to preserve the problem to which they are the solution.
meaning: The Shirky principle observes that an organisation created to solve a problem tends to develop an interest in keeping that problem alive, because its own existence depends on the problem's persistence. A body that fully solved the problem it addresses would put itself out of work, so complex institutions and industries can end up perpetuating the very difficulty they were built to relieve. It is a caution about how mission and self-interest quietly diverge.
mechanism: An institution draws its funding, headcount, status, and reason to exist from the problem it manages. That creates a standing incentive to manage the problem rather than end it, since a solved problem removes the institution's justification. The pull need not be cynical or conscious; it emerges from ordinary self-preservation and the selection pressures inside organisations. It is close kin to the iron law of bureaucracy, in which those devoted to the organisation come to outweigh those devoted to its stated goal, and to regulatory capture, where a body comes to serve its own continuation.

examples.text: An agency or department whose budget scales with the size of a problem has little incentive to shrink that problem out of existence, since doing so would shrink itself.
A business or profession that profits from an ongoing difficulty benefits more from managing it indefinitely than from a cure that would end the demand.
The related warning that it is hard to get someone to understand something when their salary depends on their not understanding it captures the same incentive.

variants.name: The naming
variants.text: Kevin Kelly coined the label 'the Shirky principle' in 2010, crediting the underlying idea to Clay Shirky and comparing its clarity to the Peter principle.

variants.name: Regulatory capture
variants.text: The economic cousin in which regulators come to serve the incumbents they oversee, or their own survival, rather than the public interest they were meant to protect.

whyItMatters: It is a memorable lens on organisational behaviour, incentives, and technological disruption, explaining why incumbents resist changes that would render them unnecessary and why some problems outlive every apparent means to solve them. It sharpens analysis of bureaucracies, industries, and reform efforts, prompting the question of who benefits from a problem continuing.

working.text: ask whether an institution's funding and status depend on the problem it addresses persisting, which predicts resistance to a real solution.
distinguish what an organisation was created to do from what keeps it alive, since the two can quietly diverge.
expect bodies to resist changes that would obviate them, and design incentives that reward solving the problem, not managing it.

limits: It is an aphorism and heuristic, observational and hard to falsify as stated, offering a lens rather than a prediction with scope or magnitude. Not every institution behaves this way; many do solve or reduce their problems, and the principle names a tendency, not a certainty. Its provenance is a small tangle worth keeping straight: Clay Shirky expressed the idea, reportedly in a talk, while Kevin Kelly created and named the principle after him.
misreadings: Shirky did not coin 'the Shirky principle'; Kevin Kelly created the label in 2010 and named it after Shirky, who supplied the idea. Nor did Kelly originate the thought; he credited Shirky. And the exact sentence is Kelly's rendering of an idea Shirky voiced in a talk, not a line lifted from a specific Shirky essay.
origin: The idea is credited to the writer Clay Shirky; the label 'the Shirky principle' was coined by Kevin Kelly in an April 2010 post on his blog The Technium, naming it after Shirky.

sources.text: Kevin Kelly, "The Shirky Principle," The Technium (2010). — the statement and Kelly's naming of the principle after Shirky.
Clay Shirky, "The Collapse of Complex Business Models" (2010). — the thematically related argument about institutions and simplification.
